grading: One point per question; one correct option; all four options include individual feedback.

questions.q: After a route change, the first GRE packets use WAN2 but NP7-offloaded packets remain on WAN1. Which design change addresses this?
c: Enable loopback ECMP offload when creating a replacement GRE tunnel.
Increase the GRE keepalive interval and leave the offload settings unchanged.
Add a second firewall policy with a higher sequence number for GRE.
Change the remote gateway address to the next-hop IP of WAN2.
f: Correct: the creation-time loopback-ecmp-offload option enables ECMP hashing for NP7-offloaded GRE over a software loopback.
Keepalive controls tunnel liveness, not the ECMP hash path used by offloaded sessions.
A second policy does not change the GRE tunnel's NP7 ECMP hashing behavior.
The remote gateway identifies the tunnel peer; it should not be rewritten to chase an underlay next hop.

questions.q: Several inner flows share one GRE tunnel over an aggregate link. Which setting adds inner L4 entropy to the LAG hash?
c: Set lag-hash-gre to gre_inner_l4 and select NPU-GRE on the aggregate.
Set loopback-ecmp-offload to enable and leave the LAG algorithm unchanged.
Set the health-check class-id to the aggregate interface's traffic class.
Disable ASIC offload on every policy that forwards the GRE traffic.
f: Correct: gre_inner_l4 uses inner transport headers, and NPU-GRE selects that configured hashing behavior for the LAG.
Loopback ECMP offload enables routed-path hashing for GRE; it does not configure aggregate member hashing.
A health-check class ID controls shaping for probes, not GRE flow hashing.
Disabling offload is a legacy workaround, not the desired inner-header LAG distribution design.

questions.q: A GRE tunnel already exists without loopback-ecmp-offload. The CLI rejects changing that option. What is the supported planning response?
c: Clear all sessions and retry the same tunnel object after the route converges.
Recreate the GRE tunnel with the option enabled and migrate traffic deliberately.
Change the loopback interface address and retain the existing GRE object.
Set the LAG algorithm to NPU-GRE, which updates the tunnel property.
f: Clearing sessions does not make a creation-time GRE property mutable.
Correct: the guide states the setting cannot be changed after tunnel creation, so plan a replacement tunnel.
Changing the loopback address does not change the immutable offload setting.
NPU-GRE configures aggregate hashing and does not rewrite the GRE object's ECMP option.

questions.q: On an older release without loopback GRE ECMP offload, which documented workaround sacrifices hardware acceleration?
c: Increase the route distance of the old WAN until all sessions expire.
Set the GRE keepalive interval to one second and retain NP7 offload.
Disable auto-asic-offload in the GRE forwarding firewall policy.
Disable ECMP globally so the software route cannot change.
f: Route distance changes the preferred route but does not fix the NP7 offload path behavior.
Keepalive frequency detects peer reachability; it does not alter ASIC forwarding eligibility.
Correct: disabling auto-asic-offload avoids the stale fast-path behavior but moves traffic away from NP7 acceleration.
Disabling ECMP globally is broader than necessary and does not provide the documented targeted workaround.

questions.q: A FortiGate already has a newer signature package. Operations wants to freeze future updates without rolling back that device. Which choice is correct?
c: Choose Downgrade so the device keeps its current package version.
Set the preferred version and choose Just Set Preferred Version.
Leave Latest selected and disable policy-package installation schedules.
Delete the package from FortiManager and let the device retry.
f: Downgrade actively changes devices that already run a later package version.
Correct: pin-only changes the future delivery ceiling while leaving a newer installed package untouched.
Policy-package schedules are separate from FortiGuard object-package version selection.
Deleting the package does not implement a controlled preferred-version policy and can disrupt updates.

questions.q: The required FortiGuard package is absent from the Receive Status list. What should the administrator check before concluding it is unavailable?
c: Clear Show Used Objects Only, then search the package list again.
Change the FortiGate ADOM to Advanced Device Mode immediately.
Reinstall the FortiManager firmware to rebuild all package records.
Create a new firewall policy package with the same package name.
f: Correct: the guide instructs administrators to clear Show Used Objects Only before searching for the package.
ADOM device mode governs device/VDOM assignment, not whether a FortiGuard package is hidden by the filter.
A firmware reinstall is unnecessary before checking the documented list filter.
Firewall policy packages are unrelated objects and do not expose FortiGuard package versions.

questions.q: What retention assumption should be checked when designing a rollback plan for FortiGuard object packages?
c: FortiManager stores every historical package version indefinitely by default.
Each managed FortiGate stores all FortiGuard package versions in its local database.
Only one package version can be retained for each object type.
FortiManager retains a maximum of 20 object versions by default.
f: The documentation does not promise indefinite package history.
The retention setting described is on FortiManager, not an unlimited local archive on each FortiGate.
More than one package version is retained; the documented default maximum is 20.
Correct: confirm the required rollback version is still within the retained version set.

questions.q: After pin-only selection, one device still reports a package version newer than the preferred version. How should this be interpreted?
c: The device is necessarily out of sync and must be reinstalled.
The preferred version only affects policy packages, not FortiGuard.
That is expected until an explicit downgrade is selected.
FortiManager will automatically downgrade it at the next full policy install.
f: A newer installed version is allowed under the pin-only choice.
The setting specifically controls FortiGuard package versions served by FortiManager.
Correct: Just Set Preferred Version does not downgrade already newer devices.
Policy installation is not the trigger for this FortiGuard package rollback workflow.

questions.q: The SNMP manager can poll FortiAnalyzer but receives no log-disk alerts. Which configuration path should be checked first?
c: Enable trap delivery for the SNMPv3 user, add its host, and select the event.
Replace the FortiAnalyzer MIB with the standard MIB-II file only.
Change the query port from UDP/161 to the trap destination port.
Restart SQL analytics before testing SNMP event notifications.
f: Correct: polling and traps are separate; the user needs trap enablement, a notification host, and the event subscription.
MIB-II alone does not decode Fortinet enterprise events and cannot enable trap delivery.
UDP/161 is the normal query port; trap delivery normally uses UDP/162 or its configured remote port.
SQL analytics is unrelated to the SNMP agent's event-subscription configuration.

questions.q: Which SNMPv3 level protects both message authenticity and payload privacy?
c: No Authentication, No Privacy with a restricted source address.
Authentication, No Privacy with an SHA-family algorithm.
Authentication and Privacy with an authentication and encryption algorithm.
Community-based v1/v2c access with a longer community string.
f: This level provides neither cryptographic authentication nor payload privacy.
Authentication protects integrity/identity but does not encrypt the SNMP payload.
Correct: authentication plus privacy combines message authentication with encryption.
A longer v1/v2c community string does not provide SNMPv3 privacy.

questions.q: A manager sends SNMP GET requests and receives responses. Which port pairing is normally expected for query and trap paths?
c: Queries use UDP/162 and traps use UDP/161.
Queries and traps both use UDP/161 by default.
Queries use TCP/161 and traps use TCP/162.
Queries use UDP/161 and traps use UDP/162.
f: The normal query and trap port roles are reversed in this option.
The default trap remote port is distinct from the query port.
The documented SNMP transport is UDP, not this TCP pairing.
Correct: FortiAnalyzer documents UDP/161 for queries and UDP/162 for traps by default.

questions.q: Traps arrive but the monitoring console displays raw enterprise OIDs. What dependency is most likely missing?
c: The FortiAnalyzer SQL database needs a new event handler.
The matching Fortinet Core and FortiAnalyzer MIBs are not loaded.
The SNMPv3 user needs a second authentication password.
The managed FortiGate devices need to be assigned to another ADOM.
f: SQL event handlers do not translate SNMP enterprise OIDs.
Correct: the manager needs matching vendor MIBs to decode Fortinet-specific objects and traps.
A second password is not the MIB decoding dependency.
ADOM assignment does not decode the SNMP trap payload.

questions.q: A bound custom command does not run after a differential port configuration change. Which global mode changes that trigger?
c: Set switch-custom-cmd to on-any.
Set switch-custom-cmd to on-replay.
Execute the command once with execute switch-controller custom-command.
Remove the per-switch binding and recreate the script name.
f: Correct: on-any pushes bound custom commands after any managed-switch configuration change.
On-replay is the default and waits for a full configuration replay.
One-time execution is not the persistent trigger for future configuration changes.
Removing the binding prevents the command from following that switch's configuration lifecycle.

questions.q: A custom command was executed once and the setting disappeared after a switch restart. What should have been used?
c: A second one-time execution immediately before the reboot.
A FortiGate firewall automation stitch with the same command text.
A bound custom-command entry under the managed-switch serial.
A new FortiLink VLAN with the script stored as its description.
f: Repeating a one-time command still does not make it part of managed configuration.
An automation stitch is not the documented binding mechanism for FortiSwitch custom commands.
Correct: bind the named command to the managed-switch serial for configuration lifecycle delivery.
A VLAN description does not store or execute a switch CLI script.

questions.q: How are line breaks represented inside the custom command string in the documented FortiGate controller syntax?
c: Use a semicolon after each command and omit the line separators.
Use the literal %0a sequence between command lines.
Use a JSON array of commands under config switch-controller custom-command.
Use a carriage-return escape that the switch controller inserts automatically.
f: A semicolon is not the documented line-break representation for this command string.
Correct: the FortiLink guide uses %0a to represent a return/newline in the stored script.
The documented object stores a command string rather than a JSON command array.
The guide explicitly demonstrates %0a rather than relying on an automatic carriage return.

questions.q: When on-any is selected, at what point are bound custom commands pushed relative to normal managed-switch configuration?
c: Before the controller validates the managed-switch serial number.
Only after a full configuration replay completes.
At the same time as each individual configuration command.
Last, after the other configuration changes have been pushed.
f: The documented sequence does not place custom commands before target binding validation.
That describes on-replay behavior, not on-any.
The guide explicitly states the custom commands are pushed last.
Correct: on-any triggers after any configuration change and sends the custom commands last.

questions.q: A DHCP server must distinguish both the AP/SSID circuit and the individual wireless station. Which Option 82 design fits?
c: Put AP/SSID fields in Circuit ID and client MAC in Remote ID.
Put client MAC in Circuit ID and use no Remote ID field.
Put the DHCP scope name in Remote ID and omit Circuit ID.
Disable insertion and rely on the station's requested IP address.
f: Correct: Circuit ID carries AP/circuit context, while Remote ID can carry the client MAC.
This reverses the documented purpose and leaves no distinct remote-host identifier.
The server's scope name is not the documented FortiAP Remote ID source.
The requested address does not provide the AP/SSID identity Option 82 is designed to add.

questions.q: Which minimum FortiAP firmware requirement applies to the customizable Option 82 feature described in the 8.0 guide?
c: FortiAP 7.4.0 or later on every supported radio.
FortiAP 7.6.2 or later only for Wi-Fi 7 radios.
FortiAP 7.6.4 or later.
FortiAP 8.0.0 only, with no earlier supported firmware.
f: The source specifies a later minimum than 7.4.0.
The feature requirement is not limited to Wi-Fi 7 radios in the source.
Correct: FortiAP firmware 7.6.4 or later is required.
The guide states 7.6.4 or later, not exclusively 8.0.0.

questions.q: Several Circuit ID sub-options are concatenated, but the DHCP server's policy does not match. What should be validated?
c: The WTP profile's radio power setting and DFS channel list.
The DHCP lease duration and the AP's management address.
The client's RSSI threshold and roaming preference values.
The selected Circuit ID fields and the configured delimiter.
f: Radio power and DFS settings do not determine the Option 82 string format.
Lease duration and management IP do not explain a Circuit ID parser mismatch.
RSSI and roaming policy are separate from DHCP relay-agent metadata.
Correct: the server must parse the exact field combination and delimiter inserted by the VAP.

questions.q: What does successful Option 82 insertion prove, and what does it not prove?
c: It proves the DHCP server has granted the client an address.
It proves metadata was inserted, not that the server selected the intended scope.
It proves the client completed 802.1X and received a production VLAN.
It proves the AP has a valid CAPWAP DTLS session to the controller.
f: Option 82 insertion occurs in the request path before the server's lease decision.
Correct: inspect the server's received fields and scope decision separately.
DHCP Option 82 does not prove 802.1X authentication or VLAN authorization.
CAPWAP control-channel health is independent of the DHCP server's scope selection.

questions.q: The Groups page shows a nonzero count but returns HTTP 500; output.master repeats recursive group-node calls. What is the likely defect?
c: A missing SNMP community prevents the group table from loading.
An LDAP realm cannot resolve the current administrator's username.
The number of groups exceeds the default display threshold only.
A self-referencing or reciprocal group membership creates a traversal cycle.
f: SNMP monitoring does not control the Groups hierarchy renderer.
A realm lookup failure would not explain recursive group-node calls.
A large group count may slow rendering, but StackOverflowError points to unbounded recursion.
Correct: the membership graph contains a cycle that prevents recursive traversal from terminating.

questions.q: Which read-only database condition directly identifies a group that contains itself?
c: PARENT_ID equals CHILD_ID for an active group-membership row.
The group name appears in two different policy mapping records.
The group owner field contains the system administrator name.
The group has more than 2,000 members in the Members column.
f: Correct: the documented self-reference query checks PARENT_ID = CHILD_ID with active group rows.
Duplicate policy references do not prove a self-loop in the membership graph.
Ownership metadata is unrelated to the parent/child relationship.
A large member count is not equivalent to a self-referential edge.

questions.q: Which group hierarchy behavior is documented and should be preserved when organizing policy objects?
c: Groups can contain subgroups of any type without restriction.
Groups are flat lists and cannot contain other groups.
Groups can contain same-type subgroups and be used for policies or roles.
Groups automatically inherit every policy assigned to their parent.
f: The guide describes same-type subgroup membership, not unrestricted cross-type nesting.
Groups are explicitly documented as able to contain other groups.
Correct: groups organize like items and can be used to assign policies or roles.
The source does not define automatic inheritance of every parent policy.

questions.q: The database contains more than 2,000 valid groups and the UI asks whether to display them. How should this differ from a cycle diagnosis?
c: Treat every delayed list as a Java StackOverflowError.
Use filters to reduce the displayed set before loading all groups.
Delete older groups directly from the database to restore the UI.
Disable group nesting globally and recreate all policy mappings.
f: A large list prompt is documented behavior and does not itself indicate recursive failure.
Correct: filter the list when the count threshold prompts for confirmation.
Direct database deletion is not a safe first-line group-management action.
Disabling nesting globally is unnecessary and would disrupt valid group structures.

questions.q: An MDM record contains Corporate ownership. Which optional connector feature can map that value into the FortiNAC Host Role?
c: Enable Update Hosts Role on the supported MDM service connector.
Enable Revalidate Health Status On Connect for every host.
Enable Automatic Registration Polling and disable role filters.
Change the endpoint's MAC address to match the MDM Device ID.
f: Correct: Update Hosts Role uses the MDM Ownership value to determine Host Role.
Health-status revalidation refreshes compliance state, not the ownership-to-role mapping.
Automatic polling can ingest records but does not replace the role-update setting.
The mapping uses MDM ownership data, not a rewritten MAC address.

questions.q: The connector is enabled, but a manually assigned Host Role remains unchanged after MDM polling. What explains this?
c: The MDM connector can update only the logged-on username field.
The Host Role field is read-only for every registered endpoint.
The MDM record must include the endpoint's current switch port name.
Only NAC-Default or unassigned Host Roles are eligible for override.
f: The connector can update Host Role from ownership when the documented option is enabled.
The Host Role is a policy attribute and is not universally read-only.
The switch port name is not the ownership-to-role mapping input.
Correct: a manually assigned non-default role is protected from automatic override.

questions.q: Which evidence chain best proves that ownership-based role mapping changed network access?
c: MDM connector test passes and the endpoint has an IP address.
Host View shows Host Role, then profile match, then resulting access policy.
The MDM portal displays Corporate ownership without checking FortiNAC.
A successful RADIUS Access-Accept proves the intended role was selected.
f: A connection test proves API reachability, not the role or policy outcome.
Correct: verify the host role, the matching profile, and the resulting enforcement separately.
The source MDM value does not prove FortiNAC ingested or mapped it.
RADIUS acceptance alone does not prove the expected User/Host Profile matched.

questions.q: Many FortiNAC servers managed by one Manager need the same MDM host records. Which deployment reduces repeated MDM API polling?
c: Configure a separate MDM connector on every managed server.
Disable MDM polling and rely on endpoint agents to populate ownership.
Configure the connector on the Manager so it copies records after each poll.
Configure only the captive portal and let the switch query MDM directly.
f: Per-server connectors create more polling activity against the MDM service.
Agent scans do not replace the documented MDM service connector data path.
Correct: Manager-level polling can copy MDM host records to managed servers after each poll.
The switch does not directly query the MDM service through the captive portal.

questions.q: A GCC High tenant fails when FortiAuthenticator's Azure Directory OAuth source calls Graph. Which architecture is documented as the supported alternative?
c: Use the commercial Azure Graph endpoint and change only the OAuth secret.
Replace SAML with RADIUS accounting proxy for the same browser session.
Use FortiAuthenticator as a SAML IdP proxy to the Government tenant.
Disable certificate validation and retain the existing Azure OAuth source.
f: Changing the secret does not change the hardcoded commercial Graph endpoint.
RADIUS accounting proxy is not a browser-based SAML federation substitute.
Correct: the current guide recommends FAC SAML IdP proxying for Azure Government.
Disabling certificate validation does not resolve the unsupported graph.microsoft.us endpoint.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the two trust boundaries in the FAC SAML proxy design?
c: FAC trusts the upstream Government IdP, then issues an assertion to the downstream SP.
The downstream SP connects directly to the Government Graph API for group data.
FAC forwards the upstream assertion unchanged without a downstream IdP relationship.
The browser authenticates to the SP first, then FAC creates a RADIUS session.
f: Correct: FAC is a proxying IdP that validates upstream authentication and serves downstream SPs.
The selected architecture avoids relying on the unsupported commercial OAuth Graph endpoint.
The downstream SP has its own trust relationship with FortiAuthenticator as IdP.
The described workflow is SAML federation, not RADIUS accounting.

questions.q: In the selected Azure Government design, what role does FortiAuthenticator present to the downstream service provider?
c: A RADIUS accounting collector that only forwards Start and Stop packets.
A SAML Identity Provider that issues the assertion trusted by the SP.
A DHCP relay agent that inserts Option 82 metadata for the endpoint.
A FortiManager FortiGuard server that distributes package versions.
f: RADIUS accounting records are not the SAML assertion interface used by the SP.
Correct: FortiAuthenticator acts as the downstream SAML IdP while proxying upstream authentication.
Option 82 is a wireless DHCP relay-agent feature unrelated to SAML.
FortiGuard package delivery is a separate FortiManager management function.

questions.q: The upstream redirect succeeds, but the downstream SP rejects the assertion. Which evidence should be checked at the FAC-to-SP boundary?
c: The FortiAnalyzer SNMP trap event list and query port.
The FortiGate GRE tunnel's loopback-ecmp-offload setting.
The FortiNAC Host Role and MDM ownership field.
The assertion issuer, audience, NameID, signature, and ACS values.
f: SNMP traps do not validate SAML issuer or audience claims.
GRE offload has no bearing on SAML assertion validation.
Host Role mapping is not part of the FAC-to-SP SAML trust boundary.
Correct: inspect the downstream assertion's trust and recipient fields separately from upstream authentication.

questions.q: Which password changer type supports the reconciliation feature described in FortiPAM 1.9?
c: SSH password changer for any Unix account template.
Active Directory LDAP password changer.
Web launcher password changer for browser-based targets.
Generic REST secret template with an arbitrary target endpoint.
f: The guide limits password reconciliation to Active Directory LDAP password changers.
Correct: the feature is explicitly supported for the Active Directory LDAP changer type.
A launcher is a connection method, not the documented reconciliation engine.
The feature is not a generic recovery mechanism for arbitrary REST templates.

questions.q: Why is a separate Reconcile Account configured for an out-of-sync base secret?
c: It acts as the privileged bind identity that can reset the base account password.
It stores the old password so FortiPAM can retry the same failed login.
It replaces the base account in every application launcher session.
It disables the target account until the next scheduled rotation.
f: Correct: the reconcile account binds with sufficient rights to reset the base account password.
Reconciliation is a reset path, not merely replaying the old failed credential.
The reconcile secret does not replace the managed base account in all sessions.
The feature recovers or resets credentials; it does not inherently disable the account.

questions.q: What is the behavioral difference between the two Activate on choices?
c: Both modes always run only after an automatic password verification succeeds.
Reconcile directly waits for a failed check-in; the other mode runs at creation.
Reconcile directly performs reconciliation instead of a normal change; the other runs after change failure.
One mode applies only to SSH secrets and the other only to LDAP secrets.
f: The activation choices are not defined by automatic verification success.
The source describes direct reconciliation versus reconciliation after password-change failure.
Correct: the two modes determine whether reconciliation is direct or failure-triggered.
Both choices are part of the supported Active Directory LDAP password reconciliation workflow.

questions.q: Which operations can be influenced by the Password Reconciliation configuration?
c: Only manual password changes initiated from the secret details window.
Only the scheduled password rotation job and never check-in.
Only verification tests after a user checks out a secret.
Manual changes, automatic changes, and password changes during secret check-in.
f: The documented effect extends beyond manual changes.
Automatic password changes are also included in the documented scope.
Check-in password changes are explicitly affected by reconciliation configuration.
Correct: the guide names all three change paths.

questions.q: A raw historical event contains an interface name inside a message, but the parser did not create a field. Which query function helps recover one value?
c: EXTRACT applied to the string-valued event attribute with a regex pattern.
EMA applied to the message field without a time aggregation.
COUNT DISTINCT applied to the entire raw event payload.
IF applied to the event timestamp without a comparison expression.
f: Correct: EXTRACT can pull one value from a string attribute in supported Analytics queries.
EMA is a moving average and requires numerical input plus time aggregation.
COUNT DISTINCT aggregates values; it does not parse a missing field from a message.
IF derives a value from a logical condition and requires an expression.

questions.q: An EMA query fails because the result has no supported time bucket. What should be added?
c: A second event parser that writes the average into the raw log.
A time aggregation field such as receive hour, date, week, or month.
A rule threshold that converts the query into an EventDB rule.
A lookup-table function that supplies a static timestamp for each event.
f: A parser change is not the documented requirement for the EMA query.
Correct: EMA requires a supported time aggregation field in the query.
Rules/EventDB are not the supported context for the new query-function set.
A static timestamp does not create the required time-series aggregation.

questions.q: Where should the new query-function pipeline be run according to the release notes?
c: Only in EventDB rules that execute on every incoming event.
Only in report templates after a PDF has been generated.
In ClickHouse or Elasticsearch Analytics queries, not EventDB queries or rules.
In any query engine as long as the function names are capitalized.
f: The release notes explicitly exclude EventDB queries and rules for the new function set.
Report rendering is not the query-engine context for these functions.
Correct: ClickHouse and Elasticsearch Analytics queries are the supported contexts described.
Function availability is engine-specific; capitalization does not make unsupported contexts valid.

questions.q: A nested expression works in ClickHouse but fails in Elasticsearch. What is the best next step?
c: Assume the query cache is stale and restart every Collector.
Convert all function calls to EventDB syntax and rerun the rule.
Increase the time window until the nested expression is accepted.
Check the engine-specific nested-function categories and depth limitations.
f: A cache restart is not the first diagnostic for a documented scope difference.
EventDB does not provide the same new query-function support.
Changing the time window does not resolve unsupported nesting categories.
Correct: nesting support differs by engine and function category.

questions.q: A laptop repeatedly starts FortiSASE tunnel attempts before its captive portal has granted Internet access. Which profile setting can cause this?
c: Disable internet check is enabled, bypassing the readiness gate.
Endpoint connects to FortiSASE VPN is set to Manually.
The SASE PoP has a shorter IPsec DPD idle interval.
The endpoint's User/Host Profile has a NAC-Default role.
f: Correct: enabling Disable internet check starts autoconnect without verifying Internet reachability.
Manual mode does not initiate automatic tunnel attempts at login.
DPD monitors an established peer and does not control the pre-connectivity check.
NAC Host Role is a FortiNAC policy attribute, not the FortiSASE local Internet check.

questions.q: What happens when Disable internet check is left disabled in an automatic FortiSASE connection profile?
c: FortiClient starts the tunnel immediately regardless of local connectivity.
FortiClient waits until Internet connectivity is confirmed before autoconnect.
FortiClient skips authentication and connects to the nearest PoP.
FortiClient switches to manual mode until the user opens the portal.
f: Immediate tunnel attempts without a check occur when the Disable internet check toggle is enabled.
Correct: the default behavior gates autoconnect on confirmed Internet reachability.
The setting does not bypass the tunnel's authentication process.
The toggle does not change the profile from automatic to manual mode.

questions.q: Where is the Internet-check behavior configured for the endpoint?
c: In the FortiAnalyzer SNMPv3 user event-subscription list.
In the FortiGate SD-WAN performance SLA class profile.
In the FortiSASE endpoint profile's Connection tab.
In the FortiPAM secret's password reconciliation settings.
f: SNMP subscriptions monitor FortiAnalyzer system events, not endpoint connectivity.
SD-WAN class profiles prioritize probes on WAN egress interfaces.
Correct: the Connection tab contains the endpoint tunnel autoconnect and Internet-check options.
Password reconciliation controls managed account credentials, not VPN startup.

questions.q: A tunnel is already established and then begins failing peer-liveness checks. Is the Internet-check toggle the correct control?
c: Yes; it changes the interval of established tunnel DPD probes.
Yes; it rewrites the endpoint's SAML assertion audience.
No; the toggle gates autoconnect before tunnel establishment, not DPD.
No; it changes the FortiSASE Security PoP's DNS geolocation.
f: The Internet-check setting is not the DPD timer for an established tunnel.
SAML audience validation is unrelated to local Internet reachability gating.
Correct: once a tunnel exists, diagnose DPD and tunnel liveness separately.
DNS geolocation is not controlled by this endpoint profile toggle.

questions.q: Which command assigns a health-check's probes to a traffic class?
c: set sla-fail-log-period 30 under the health-check object.
set class-id 2 under the SD-WAN health-check object.
set diffservcode 46 under the interface's IPv6 configuration.
set fortiguard-name to the selected probe destination.
f: SLA fail-log period controls logging intervals, not packet classification.
Correct: the class-id parameter assigns the health-check probes to a traffic class.
Diffservcode marking and IPv6 interface settings are not the documented class-id mapping.
FortiGuard target selection defines a probe destination, not an egress scheduler class.

questions.q: What must exist for an SLA probe class ID to receive guaranteed bandwidth during egress congestion?
c: A matching traffic class, shaping-profile entry, and egress profile on the member.
A second health-check server and a longer probe timeout.
A BGP community that maps the SLA name to a route tag.
A firewall policy with a higher sequence number than user traffic.
f: Correct: the class ID must map to a configured shaping class and an egress shaping profile.
More probe servers improve destination redundancy, not scheduler bandwidth guarantees.
BGP route tags influence routing policy and do not create egress class guarantees.
Policy sequence does not configure the traffic-class scheduler.

questions.q: Which output best proves that probe packets are entering the intended egress traffic class?
c: diagnose sys sdwan health-check showing state(alive) only.
get router info routing-table all showing both WAN defaults.
diagnose netlink interface list showing the class counter increasing.
show firewall policy showing the SD-WAN rule name.
f: Health-check state proves probe response, not scheduler classification.
A routing table shows available routes, not traffic-class counters.
Correct: netlink output exposes class allocation, priority, and forwarded-byte counters.
A firewall policy name does not prove which shaping class carried the probes.

questions.q: The health-check reports packet loss, but the engineer needs to prove the probe class is protected under congestion. What evidence is still needed?
c: Only a successful DNS lookup to the probe server.
Only a green status arrow in the SD-WAN GUI.
Only a route-table entry for each SD-WAN member.
Egress class allocation, priority, and probe-class forwarded-byte counters.
f: DNS resolution proves name service, not egress scheduling.
A green status indicator does not prove class assignment or guaranteed bandwidth.
A route entry does not show the scheduler treatment of probe packets.
Correct: inspect netlink class bandwidth and counters alongside the health-check metrics.

questions.q: FortiAnalyzer emits a CPU-overuse SNMP trap, but the team claims this proves all incoming FortiGate logs are indexed. Is that conclusion valid?
c: Yes; an appliance trap confirms log ingestion and SQL indexing completed.
No; the trap proves a system event, so log ingestion and Analytics need separate checks.
Yes; SNMPv3 traps are generated only after the Analytics database commits each log.
No; SNMP traps can only be generated by managed FortiGate devices.
f: A CPU trap is not an end-to-end log-ingestion acknowledgement.
Correct: system SNMP notifications and log receive/index pipelines are separate evidence paths.
The SNMP agent emits appliance events; it is not a per-log database commit hook.
FortiAnalyzer's own SNMP agent can emit traps originating on the appliance.

questions.q: A FortiSASE tunnel does not start while the endpoint is offline. Why is changing DPD not the first troubleshooting step?
c: DPD operates after a tunnel exists; first inspect the endpoint Internet-check gate.
DPD controls the FortiGate NP7 GRE loopback ECMP hash selection.
DPD determines whether FortiManager serves Latest or a pinned package.
DPD assigns FortiNAC Host Roles from the MDM ownership value.
f: Correct: pre-connectivity gating occurs before tunnel establishment; DPD is a peer-liveness mechanism for an existing tunnel.
NP7 GRE ECMP hashing is unrelated to FortiSASE endpoint DPD.
FortiGuard package version selection is a FortiManager management workflow.
MDM ownership-to-role mapping is a FortiNAC-F policy attribute feature.
